issues.legal_issue: A memorandum accompanying a deposit of title deeds requires registration when the parties intend it to embody their bargain and create the mortgage.
material_facts: The bank relied on an unregistered printed form signed in connection with the deposit of title deeds.
The form was incomplete because unnecessary printed terms had not been struck out.
The form described itself as recording terms already agreed upon.
issues.conclusion: A document intended to embody the mortgage bargain requires registration; this document was not intended to do so and was only evidential.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 17 of the Registration Act, 1908, a document that embodies the bargain creating a mortgage by deposit of title deeds must be registered. Where the parties do not intend the document to embody their bargain, the mortgage arises by implication from the deposit with the requisite intention, and a merely evidential memorandum need not be registered. The Court applied Rachpal Maharaj v. Bhagwandas Daruka, Pranjivandas Mehta v. Chan Ma Phee, Shaw v. Foster, and Subramonian v. Lutchman.

predicates.mortgage_by_title_deposit: The parties deposited title deeds with a creditor intending to create security over the property.
predicates.written_bargain_intended: The parties intended their written document itself to embody the bargain creating the security.

issues.definition: When title deeds are deposited to create security and the parties intend their writing to embody that bargain, the writing requires registration.

issues.legal_issue: Further evidence may be used to test the recitals in a document that merely records a deposit of title deeds made under an earlier agreement.
material_facts: The bank relied on an unregistered document that, by its recitals, recorded terms already agreed upon.
The document was treated as a memorandum evidencing the deposit rather than as the contract creating the mortgage.
issues.conclusion: If the document was merely a memorandum, the correctness of its recitals could be examined using further evidence, without that evidence being barred by sections 91 and 92 of the Evidence Act, 1872.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 91 and 92 of the Evidence Act, 1872 do not prevent further evidence from being considered to test the recitals of a document that is merely evidential and does not itself embody the parties’ contract. The Court also relied on Rachpal Maharaj v. Bhagwandas Daruka and the principles discussed in Pranjivandas Mehta v. Chan Ma Phee, Shaw v. Foster, and Subramonian v. Lutchman.

predicates.mortgage_by_title_deposit: The parties deposited title deeds with a creditor intending to create security over the property.
predicates.memorandum_only: The document records a deposit made under an earlier agreement and does not itself embody the parties’ bargain.

issues.definition: If a document only records an earlier agreement accompanying a title-deed deposit, further evidence may be used to test the document’s recitals.

issues.legal_issue: A decree enforcing a title-deed mortgage against a depositor cannot stand when the deeds were not deposited to secure the debts claimed against that depositor.
material_facts: The appeal concerned a decree against a depositor based on title deeds deposited with a bank.
The evidence showed that the depositor had obtained a separate loan for his own business, secured by the title deeds.
The records and correspondence concerning the other borrowers’ debts did not identify the deposited deeds as security for those debts.
The bank produced no reliable evidence, apart from the disputed memorandum, that the deeds were intended to secure those debts.
On an overall assessment of the evidence and probabilities, the Court found that the deeds had not been deposited to secure the debts claimed against the depositor.
issues.conclusion: The decree against the depositor was set aside and the suit against him was dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: A mortgage by deposit of title deeds depends on the requisite intention to create security for the debt in question. The Court assessed that intention from the document’s nature and wording, the surrounding circumstances, and the available evidence; it relied on Rachpal Maharaj v. Bhagwandas Daruka and the related principles in Pranjivandas Mehta v. Chan Ma Phee, Shaw v. Foster, and Subramonian v. Lutchman.

predicates.appeal_against_money_decree: The proceeding is an appeal challenging a money decree imposed on a person said to have secured another debt with deposited title deeds.
predicates.title_deeds_not_intended_to_secure_claim: The title deeds were not deposited with the intention of securing the debt for which enforcement is sought against the depositor.
predicates.no_reliable_independent_support: No reliable evidence independent of the disputed document supports the claimed intention to secure that debt.

issues.definition: In an appeal against a money decree, if the deeds were not intended to secure the claimed debt and reliable independent evidence does not support that security, the decree against the depositor cannot stand.
